issues.legal_issue: A conviction for a serious offence may rest on circumstantial evidence only when the prosecution proves guilt beyond reasonable doubt through a complete chain that excludes reasonable hypotheses consistent with innocence.
material_facts: All seven witnesses presented as eyewitnesses turned hostile in court, and the case was treated as one resting on circumstantial evidence.
The complainant lodged a prompt report naming the accused; he and another injured witness admitted their presence and injuries, and their medical evidence was consistent with the occurrence.

The witnesses had named the accused in their statements to the investigating officer, and the investigating officer testified to those statements and to recovery of the accused’s licensed gun at his instance.
The medical evidence recorded multiple firearm injuries to the deceased and injured persons.
The trial and High Courts had convicted the accused, and the Supreme Court considered the evidence as a whole.
issues.conclusion: The Court found no cogent reason to disturb the concurrent findings of guilt and dismissed the appeal; the conviction was sustained on the totality of the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and the burden never shifts. A serious or brutal offence calls for greater assurance and careful scrutiny, not conviction on suspicion or moral reaction. Under Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1984 SC 1622, the circumstances must be fully established, consistent only with guilt, conclusive, exclude every possible hypothesis except guilt, and form a complete chain leaving no reasonable ground consistent with innocence. The Court also relied on Kashmira Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh, AIR 1952 SC 159; State of Punjab v. Jagir Singh, AIR 1973 SC 2407; Shankarlal Gyarasilal Dixit v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1981 SC 765; Mousam Singha Roy v. State of West Bengal, (2003) 12 SCC 377; Aloke Nath Dutta v. State of West Bengal, (2007) 12 SCC 230; Sarwan Singh Rattan Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1957 SC 637; State of Uttar Pradesh v. Satish, (2005) 3 SCC 114; Krishnan v. State, (2008) 15 SCC 430; Ramesh Bhai v. State of Rajasthan, (2009) 12 SCC 603; Subramaniam v. State of Tamil Nadu, (2009) 14 SCC 415; and Babu v. State of Kerala, JT 2010 (8) SC 560.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal concerns a circumstantial case and the specified reporting, witness, medical, and recovery facts are present, the conviction is sustained.

issues.legal_issue: A witness’s evidence is not erased merely because the witness is declared hostile, and the court may rely on portions found dependable after careful scrutiny.
material_facts: The eyewitnesses did not support the prosecution in court; several denied being present, while the complainant and another injured witness admitted their presence and injuries but denied the accused’s involvement.

The complainant admitted that he had lodged the prompt report naming the accused and explained that he had named him at the urging of people in the crowd, though he said he had not seen the accused fire.
The complainant and another witness acknowledged that a family dispute concerned the division of immovable property, and witnesses testified that a Panchayat had pardoned the accused.
The witnesses’ medical examinations corroborated that the complainant and another witness had suffered injuries in the incident.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that hostile testimony was not to be rejected en bloc and could be accepted to the extent it was dependable; it found that the witnesses had concealed material facts to protect the accused.
issues.legal_principle: A hostile witness’s evidence is not effaced or washed off the record. It must be assessed as a whole and with caution, and the court should normally seek corroboration before acting on it. The Court relied on State of Gujarat v. Anirudhsing, (1997) 6 SCC 514; State of Rajasthan v. Bhawani, (2003) 7 SCC 291; Radha Mohan Singh v. State of U.P., (2006) 2 SCC 450; Mahesh v. State of Maharashtra, (2008) 13 SCC 271; Rajendra v. State of Uttar Pradesh, (2009) 13 SCC 480; and Govindappa v. State of Karnataka, (2010) 6 SCC 533.

predicates.witness_declared_hostile: A witness is declared hostile after giving evidence that departs from the prosecution account.
predicates.testimony_contains_dependable_portions: The witness’s testimony contains portions that remain dependable on careful scrutiny.

issues.definition: In a criminal trial, dependable portions of a hostile witness’s testimony may be relied on when such portions remain after careful scrutiny.

issues.legal_issue: An omission to put an incriminating circumstance to the accused during examination under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure does not by itself vitiate a conviction unless the omission causes material prejudice or a failure of justice.
material_facts: The accused argued that the trial court had not put certain circumstances to him, including recovery of the gun, motive, his absence after the offence, and the Panchayat pardon.
The trial court had asked the accused about recovery of the gun, and he denied that it had been recovered at his instance while acknowledging that he had deposited it with a dealer.
The Court held that the Panchayat pardon was not incriminating material and that absence after the offence could not itself be treated as a circumstance against the accused.
The Court found that the asserted omissions had not materially prejudiced the accused or resulted in a miscarriage of justice.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the omissions did not vitiate the conviction because they caused no material prejudice or miscarriage of justice.
issues.legal_principle: Section 313 Cr.P.C. requires the court to bring each material incriminating circumstance specifically to the accused’s attention so that the accused may explain it. An unput circumstance ordinarily must be excluded from consideration, but an omission does not automatically vitiate the trial; the accused must show material prejudice or failure of justice, and the court should seek to correct a lapse where possible. The Court relied on Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1984 SC 1622; State of Maharashtra v. Sukhdev Singh, AIR 1992 SC 2100; Wasim Khan v. State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1956 SC 400; Bhoor Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1974 SC 1256; Labhchand Dhanpat Singh Jain v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1975 SC 182; State of Punjab v. Naib Din, AIR 2001 SC 3955; Parsuram Pandey v. State of Bihar, (2004) 13 SCC 189; Asraf Ali v. State of Assam, (2008) 16 SCC 328; Shivaji Sahebrao Bobade v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1973 SC 2622; Ganesh Gogoi v. State of Assam, (2009) 7 SCC 404; Basavaraj R. Patil v. State of Karnataka, (2000) 8 SCC 740; Shaikh Maqsood v. State of Maharashtra, (2009) 6 SCC 583; Ranvir Yadav v. State of Bihar, (2009) 6 SCC 595; and Suresh Chandra Bahri v. State of Bihar, AIR 1994 SC 2420.

issues.legal_issue: A person’s absconding after an offence, by itself, does not establish guilt or complete a circumstantial chain of evidence.
material_facts: The accused was arrested six days after the offence and had remained untraceable during that period.
The lower courts considered his absence, but the Supreme Court held that it could not be used as a circumstance against him by itself.
The circumstance of absence had not been put to the accused, and the Court found that this omission was inconsequential because absence alone could not establish guilt.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that absconding alone was not proof of guilt and could not be a determining link in the circumstantial evidence chain.
issues.legal_principle: Absconding is relevant only for consideration with the other evidence and its value depends on the circumstances of the case; it is not, by itself, conclusive proof of guilt or a determining link in a circumstantial chain. The Court relied on Matru v. State of U.P., AIR 1971 SC 1050; Rahman v. State of U.P., AIR 1972 SC 110; State of M.P. v. Paltan Mallah, AIR 2005 SC 733; and Bipin Kumar Mondal v. State of West Bengal, JT 2010 (7) SC 379.

issues.legal_issue: Proof of motive may support a circumstantial case, but the absence of proof of motive alone is not a ground to reject the prosecution case.
material_facts: The alleged motive was the accused’s resentment over the allocation of family immovable property.
The accused argued that no motive or genesis of the occurrence had been established.
The Court held that motive, if proved, could supply a link in the circumstantial chain, but its absence alone did not justify rejecting the prosecution case.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the contention that the prosecution case failed because motive had not been proved.
issues.legal_principle: Motive may provide a link in a chain of circumstantial evidence, but its absence is not by itself a ground to reject the prosecution case. The Court relied on Suresh Chandra Bahri v. State of Bihar, AIR 1994 SC 2420, and State of Gujarat v. Anirudhsing, (1997) 6 SCC 514.

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding concerns a prosecution for a criminal offence.
predicates.motive_not_proved: The prosecution has not established a motive for the alleged offence.

issues.definition: In a criminal prosecution, failure to prove motive alone does not defeat the prosecution case.

issues.legal_issue: A family or community pardon does not determine criminal responsibility for a heinous offence against society.
material_facts: Witnesses testified that a Panchayat had convened and pardoned the accused after the incident.
The Court found that the Panchayat decision explained why the eyewitnesses had turned hostile.
The alleged offences involved the deaths of three people and injuries to three others.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the family and Panchayat pardon had no significance to the prosecution of the alleged heinous crime against society.
issues.legal_principle: A private or community pardon cannot extinguish the public character of a heinous crime committed against society or the State; in this case, the Court treated the pardon as an explanation for the witnesses’ hostility, not as a circumstance proving the offence. The judgment states this principle in its application to the facts and does not cite a separate authority for it.

predicates.heinous_criminal_case: The proceeding concerns an alleged heinous criminal offence against society.
predicates.family_or_community_pardons_accused: The accused’s family or community purports to pardon the accused for the offence.

issues.definition: In a prosecution for a heinous offence against society, a family or community pardon does not affect the criminal prosecution.
